segments.titre: Ozempic changes what obesity means
segments.resume: In 2012 a weekly injection matching gastric bypass would have seemed absurd. Ozempic then reframed obesity as a biological problem rather than a willpower one and became a cultural phenomenon, though the pharmaceutical industry already considered GLP-1 drugs old news.
segments.texte: In 2012, if you told a doctor that a weekly injection could produce the same weight loss as gastric bypass surgery, they would have laughed you out of the office. Then Ozempic arrived and changed what obesity even meant. Suddenly, being fat was a biological problem, not a willpower one. And here was a real drug that could fix it. The world went crazy. Celebrities started disappearing, then reemerging looking gaunt and skinnier than anyone could remember. Ozempic became a punchline, a miracle, and a cultural earthquake all at once. But inside the pharmaceutical industry, GLP-1 drugs, as they’re known, were already considered old news.

segments.titre: Retatrutide teaser: 30% weight loss, unapproved but already used
segments.resume: Eli Lilly built a drug that tells fat cells to burn themselves, producing about 30% weight loss versus roughly 13% for Ozempic. Retatrutide cannot be prescribed before 2028, yet biohackers and tech executives already buy it from Chinese factories that also sold fentanyl ingredients.
segments.texte: That’s because Eli Lilly, one of the world’s largest pharmaceutical companies, had been quietly building something that made Ozempic look like a prototype. Rather than telling your brain it should just stop eating, this new drug told your fat cells to actively burn themselves up. Whereas Ozempic could safely guarantee weight loss of 13% or more, the new drug produced 30%. The gap is the difference between losing 30 pounds and 90–the difference between a simple pill and a surgical outcome. It’s called Retatrutide, and you can’t get it from a doctor, at least not until 2028. And yet it’s already out there in the refrigerators of biohackers and tech executives who bought it from Chinese factories that were also selling fentanyl ingredients eight months previous. When something works this well, people don’t tend to wait for the safety manual. And today, we’re going to tell you all about it.

segments.titre: Obesity as laziness: the old medical consensus
segments.resume: For most of history obesity was seen as laziness and lack of discipline. The accepted treatment was a lecture about eating less and moving more, with bariatric surgery as the last resort.
segments.texte: For most of human history, we thought fat people were just lazy. That’s not an exaggeration, either. That was medical consensus. Eat less, move more. Calories in, calories out. If you were obese, you lacked discipline, and if a doctor said it more gently than that, the underlying assumption was the same. The treatment for obesity was essentially a lecture. Sometimes two, with bariatric surgery as a failsafe waiting in the wings if you were lucky or desperate enough.

segments.titre: 2021 semaglutide trial: 15% weight loss
segments.resume: In 2021 Novo Nordisk published results showing weekly semaglutide, sold as the diabetes drug Ozempic since 2017, produced about 15% average weight loss. For a 300-pound person that is 45 pounds in a year, far beyond diet, behavioral therapy and appetite suppressants, which gave only 3 to 5%.
segments.texte: Then, in 2021, something cracked. Novo Nordisk, a Danish pharmaceutical company most people had never heard of, published the results of a drug trial that made endocrinologists do a double take. A once-weekly injection of semaglutide, which they'd been selling as a diabetes drug called Ozempic since 2017, produced average weight loss of 15% of total body weight in obese patients. That doesn't sound radical until you do the math on a 300-pound person. That's 45 pounds lost in a single year caused by a once-weekly shot. The medical establishment at the time then entered a quiet crisis. 15% of someone’s body weight was better than anything they could recommend, better than almost anything they’d tried. Decades of clinical trials on diet interventions, behavioral therapy, and appetite suppressants had been surpassed in one fell swoop. Most of them produced 3 to 5% weight loss that patients couldn't sustain anyway. Ozempic was handily beating the field, even lapping it.

segments.titre: How GLP-1 works: hormone, brain signal and food noise
segments.resume: GLP-1, glucagon-like peptide-1, is released by the gut after eating, triggers insulin release and tells the brain it is full. In obese patients the brain receptors had dulled; semaglutide stays in the blood for seven days instead of two minutes and turns the signal up, silencing food noise.
segments.texte: The reason it worked so well came down to a hormone most people have never heard of: GLP-1, or Glucagon-like peptide-1. Your gut releases it naturally after you eat, and it does two things: First, it tells your pancreas to release insulin; and second, it tells your brain you're full. The problem, in obese patients, is that the brain's response to that signal had essentially gone quiet. The receptors had dulled. The message wasn't getting through. Semaglutide is a synthetic version of GLP-1 that stays in your bloodstream for seven days instead of two minutes. Instead of merely fixing the broken receiver, it goes ahead and turns the volume up so loud the brain can't ignore it anymore. Soon all that annoying food noise disappears. The obsessive background hum of wanting to eat, the thing that diet culture had spent fifty years telling people to resist through willpower , simply started to disappear. Soon patients on Ozempic didn’t have to white-knuckle their way through the afternoon after eating a small salad for lunch anymore. Soon they were forgetting to eat lunch altogether.

segments.titre: Ozempic goes mainstream and proves obesity is neurological
segments.resume: By 2023 Ozempic was everywhere, in jokes, gossip and congressional hearings on shortages, costing $1,000 a month and doubling Novo Nordisk's market cap. Behind the vanity narrative, it was the first pharmaceutical proof that obesity is a neurological condition, not a moral failing.
segments.texte: The world quickly took note. By 2023, Ozempic was everywhere. It inundated late night television jokes, filled celebrity gossip columns, and appeared in congressional hearings about shortages. People were paying $1,000 a month out of pocket for the stuff. Novo Nordisk's market cap doubled, then doubled again, making it the twelfth most valuable company in the world. It felt like a medical revolution. But soon the cultural story became about vanity and abuse and celebrities using a diabetes drug to lose vanity pounds. The actual medical reality was something else entirely. For the first time in history, there was pharmaceutical proof that obesity was a neurological condition, not a moral failing. The brain was misfiring. Here was a drug that could fix the misfire.

segments.titre: Eli Lilly's idea: activate three hormone receptors at once
segments.resume: Eli Lilly asked what would happen if three hormone signals were pulled at once instead of one. Rather than iterating on semaglutide, it engineered a single weekly molecule that activates the GLP-1, GIP and glucagon receptors simultaneously.
segments.texte: And then Eli Lilly showed up asking questions nobody had thought to ask. If one hormone signal produces 15% weight loss, what would happen if you decided to pull three at once? Pharmaceutical companies iterate constantly. What happens if we introduce a slightly longer half-life here, or a marginally better receptor affinity there? What Eli Lilly was proposing was far beyond iteration. They wanted to build something categorically different. Instead of adding a second or third hormone signal to semaglutide's single one, they went and engineered a molecule that activates all three receptors simultaneously–GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon, all in a single weekly injection, each one doing something the others can't.

segments.titre: What GLP-1, GIP and glucagon each do
segments.resume: GLP-1 kills food noise, GIP improves insulin sensitivity and fuel processing, and glucagon orders fat cells to burn. Glucagon is the counter-hormone to insulin that evolved to release stored fuel during famine, and retatrutide runs that signal continuously at maximum strength.
segments.texte: We’ll come back to this, but here it is in a nutshell: While GLP-1 kills the food noise, GIP optimizes insulin sensitivity, basically ensuring the body’s fuel processing machinery runs cleaner. And then there’s glucagon, the one that changes everything. If GLP-1 tells your brain to stop eating, glucagon walks directly into your fat cells and orders them to burn. This is the body’s own mobilization signal, the counter-hormone to insulin, which is the one that tells your body to “release” not “store.” And for 200,000 years of human evolution, glucagon existed to pull fuel out of storage during famine. Retatrutide hijacks that signal and runs it continuously, at maximum strength, regardless of whether there’s a famine or not.

segments.titre: Phase 3 result: retatrutide matches gastric bypass
segments.resume: Phase 3 trials show average weight loss of 28-30%, about 90 pounds for a 300-pound person in under two years. This matches gastric bypass, which averaged 28.4% over 7 years in the LABS study but requires anesthesia, rerouted digestion, supplements and carries 0.2% mortality; the drug is not approved before 2028.
segments.texte: The result, as published recently after Phase 3 trials, is weight loss averaging 28-30% of a person’s total body weight. For a 300 pound person, that is 90 pounds lost in less than two years. Consider what it might take to lose that weight any other way. You have the choice of gastric bypass surgery, one of the most invasive elective procedures in medicine which requires general anesthesia, a permanently re-routed digestive tract, and lifelong nutritional supplementation (along with a 0.2% mortality rate, mind you), all of which produces a weight loss of about 28% of body weight. A landmark LABS study tracked gastric bypass patients for 7 years, and their number hovered around 28.4%. Retatrutide just matched it, using a needle once a week for just under two years. You can forget the operating table and nutritional deficiencies for the rest of your life. The drug isn’t approved yet, and it won’t be until 2028 at the earliest. But the data exists, and data, it turns out, doesn’t wait for regulatory approval to travel.

segments.titre: The metabolism as a city: fat as emergency reserves
segments.resume: Metabolism is likened to a city of 37 trillion cells governed by the brain, with fat cells as emergency fuel silos. Fat is an evolutionary achievement for famine survival, but in modern abundance the brain keeps defending reserves, which is why dieting is a war against survival programming.
segments.texte: To get what Retatrutide actually does to your body, it helps to review what your body thinks its doing at all times. Your metabolism works like a city. A sprawling, chaotic, incredibly sophisticated city of roughly 37 trillion cells, all of them demanding energy and sending signals up the chain about supply and demand. All of these cells are dependent on a central government, your brain, which makes decisions about when to stockpile fuel and when to burn it. Fat cells are your city’s emergency fuel reserves. The silos. They exist because your body is brilliant, not broken. For as long as humans have been kicking around, their next meal was never guaranteed. A hunter-gatherer who stored fat efficiently survived droughts, famines, and long winters. A hunter-gatherer who burned through their reserves too quickly died. It was that simple. Please don’t think of fat as a design flaw. Above all, the fat cell is one of evolution’s greatest achievements, akin to a biological savings account that kept humans alive through conditions that would have killed most modern people in a week. Today, unfortunately, most people are running ancient survival hardware in a world of permanent abundance. The emergency reserves never get drawn down because the emergency never comes that will require them. And so, the silos get fuller. The savings account keeps filling. And the city's central government, the brain, keeps on defending those reserves with everything it has, because as far as it's concerned, the famine is still coming. This is why dieting is so brutally hard. It is a war against an innate survival programming that was specifically designed to make you fail. Every weight loss drug in history has tried to resolve that one fundamental problem. How to trick your body into burning the reserve tanks? Most of them have lost the war.

segments.titre: From single GLP-1 signal to tirzepatide's two signals
segments.resume: First-generation GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy sent one signal that suppressed appetite for about 15% weight loss. Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) added GIP to improve insulin sensitivity and reached over 22%, but the body slowly adapted.
segments.texte: The first GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic, Wegovy, and others won a battle. They managed to dispatch a single signal to the city, an executive order from the mayor’s office that ordered the food delivery trucks to stop their deliveries. This signal suppressed appetites until the incoming supply of fuel slowed to a manageable crawl and the brain received enough messages telling it the body was full enough. And with that, the city could start drawing down its reserves to compensate. With that comes 15% weight loss, remarkable by any prior standard. Drugs like Mounjaro, a tirzepatide, added a second dispatch signal to the signal center. GLP-1 plus GIP. This managed to stop the food trucks and retune the power grid. The GIP signal improves how efficiently the city processes whatever fuel that does come into it. It’s the machinery that determines insulin sensitivity, what decides whether incoming calories get burned or stored. Two signals is better than one, and the outcomes certainly agreed. Tests showed over 22% weight loss, an improvement over 15%. But then the city adapted, more slowly, but it adapted.

segments.titre: Retatrutide's three orders: appetite, power grid, glucagon furnaces
segments.resume: Using the city metaphor, retatrutide issues three orders at once: remove food noise, retune insulin and fuel processing, and use glucagon to turn on the fat furnaces at maximum output. Glucagon is the body's mobilization hormone used during exercise, fasting and emergencies.
segments.texte: Which is where retatrutide comes in. With this drug, the mayor shows up in person with three executive orders in hand it will issue simultaneously to the entire city. With all three, the city has no framework to resist. Order one makes the food trucks disappear. Patients in clinical trials describe the complete absence of food noise. The background static of negotiating with yourself at 10 p.m. just prior to turning into a Taco Bell drive thru, gone in a matter of weeks. Order two retunes the power grid. Whatever fuel is still coming in gets processed cleanly and without the insulin spikes and crashes that drive further hunger and fat storage. With that, the city’s entire management system becomes frictionless and functional. Order three is the glucagon. It’s the card nobody has pulled before. The order that changes everything. With this order in hand, the glucagon can walk directly to the emergency fat silos and turn on every furnace in the city. Burn everything you’ve got in storage, it says. And do it at maximum output. Glucagon is the body’s own mobilization hormone, the counter-signal to insulin. When insulin says store, glucagon says release. Your body uses it naturally during exercise, fasting, and genuine emergencies when it needs fuel fast.

segments.titre: Why the triple agonist avoids the plateau
segments.resume: The three signals balance each other: GIP smooths glucose, GLP-1 suppresses appetite and glucagon keeps burning, overriding the metabolic slowdown. Diets fail because the body fights back, with 80-95% regaining weight within 3 to 5 years, yet retatrutide showed no plateau through 80 or 104 weeks.
segments.texte: The engineering genius of the triple agonist drug is what happens when all three orders run at once. The GIP signal smooths the glucose response so the glucagon activation doesn’t spike blood sugar into dangerous territory. The GLP-1 signal keeps appetite suppressed so the body isn’t screaming at you to refuel the emptying reserves. And the glucagon signal keeps the furnaces running hot even if the body is losing weight. Together, they override the metabolic slowdown that has derailed every other weight loss intervention in history. That last part is critical. Every diet, every drug, every intervention that humanity has ever produced to cause weight loss in the species has run into the same wall. The body fights back. It’s the survival instinct. This alone is the reason that 80-95% of people who lose significant weight through diet alone regain it within three to five years. In Phase 3 trials, Retatrutide participants showed no weight loss plateau through 80 weeks. Or 104 weeks. The body has not figured out how to resist the triple signal.

segments.titre: Gila monster venom and the discovery of exendin-4
segments.resume: In the early 1990s Dr. John Eng, an endocrinologist at the Bronx VA Medical Center, studied Gila monster venom, as the lizard can go months without eating. He found exendin-4, nearly identical to GLP-1 but lasting hours instead of two minutes, and the VA declined to patent it.
segments.texte: Now none of these weight loss drugs exists without a lizard that most people have never heard of, sitting in a jar in a lab in the Bronx in the early 1990s. Dr. John Eng was an endocrinologist at the Bronx VA Medical Center, and his research subject was about as unglamorous as biomedical science gets: the venom of the Gila monster. If you've never seen one, picture a foot-long lizard covered in beaded, black-and-orange scales, native to the deserts of the American Southwest, that spends most of its life doing absolutely nothing. The Gila monster can go four to five months without eating a single meal. It survives on stored fat, through brutal desert conditions, without its blood sugar collapsing the way a human's would after even a few days of starvation. Eng wanted to know why. What he found buried in that lizard venom was a peptide called exendin-4. It looked almost identical to a human hormone called GLP-1, sound familiar? But exendin-4 had one critical difference: it lasted a long time. Human GLP-1 breaks down in your bloodstream in about two minutes. Exendin-4 survived for hours. The Gila monster, it turned out, was walking around with a built-in, slow-release version of the exact hormone that would eventually become the foundation of a trillion-dollar industry. Eng tried to get the VA to patent it, but they declined. Apparently they couldn’t see the commercial potential in a lizard hormone. Go figure.

segments.titre: From exendin-4 to Byetta, the first GLP-1 drug
segments.resume: Eng licensed the peptide to the small biotech Amylin because big pharma saw peptide drugs as impractical. In 2005 exenatide, branded Byetta, became the first FDA-approved GLP-1 agonist, needing twice-daily injections with modest results but proving the concept.
segments.texte: So Eng licensed it himself to a small biotech called Amylin Pharmaceuticals because apparently pharmaceutical giants weren’t interested in it either. Peptide drugs were still considered impractical in the ‘90s. They were expensive to manufacture and too easy for the body to break down. And so Eng’s discovery sat dormant for nearly a decade. Then in 2005, a synthetic version of exendin-4 called exenatide, rebranded as Byetta, became the first GLP-1 receptor agonist ever approved by the FDA. This required twice-daily injections, with modest results. And nobody outside endocrinology paid much attention. But at least this proved the concept valid. That was the green light for the pharmaceutical industry to do what it always does: iterate, relentlessly, for decades, until the iteration becomes a commercially viable revolution.

segments.titre: Victoza, semaglutide and tirzepatide: the iteration race
segments.resume: Novo Nordisk released liraglutide (Victoza) in 2010, a daily injection with a fatty acid chain, then semaglutide in 2017 with three molecular changes lasting seven days, sold as Ozempic and, from 2021, Wegovy for obesity. Eli Lilly followed in 2022 with tirzepatide, Mounjaro and Zepbound, targeting two receptors.
segments.texte: In 2010, Novo Nordisk released Victoza, a liraglutide injected once-daily and built from a version of human GLP-1 itself, not lizard venom. Victoza came attached with a fatty acid chain that let it bind to albumin in the blood and resist breakdown, which was nice. But it still required a daily needle to the bloodstream, which wasn’t very much fun. Then in 2017, Novo Nordisk pushed the modification even further. Three simultaneous changes were made to the molecular backbone of these GLP-1s. First was a substitution to block enzyme breakdown, another to prevent the fatty acid chain from attaching itself to the wrong place, and this to send a longer fatty diacid chain that bound the albumin even more tightly. The result was a molecule that could survive in the bloodstream for seven days instead of a few minutes. They called it semaglutide. They branded it Ozempic, a diabetes medication. In 2021, the same molecule got a higher dose and was sold under a new name: Wegovy. This was approved specifically for obesity instead of diabetes. And finally, in 2022, we come to Eli Lilly, who watched Novo Nordisk dominate a market it had quietly been building toward for years. That year, they released tirzepatide, branded Mounjaro for diabetes, and Zepbound for obesity in 2023. Two receptors instead of one, and Lilly takes the lead.

segments.titre: Novo Nordisk versus Eli Lilly: the trillion-dollar obesity market
segments.resume: Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly are in fierce competition over an obesity drug market forecast to exceed $100 billion. In 2026 Eli Lilly became the first pharmaceutical company to pass a $1 trillion valuation, while Denmark's economy depends on Novo's injection pen; Lilly now seeks to break the weight loss plateau.
segments.texte: The rivalry between Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly was anything but friendly. These are two of the largest pharmaceutical companies on Earth, locked in direct competition over what has become one of the most valuable drug categories in human history. The global obesity medicines market was worthv in 2025. It's forecast to exceed $100 billion within two years. In 2026, Eli Lilly became the first pharmaceutical company in history to cross a $1 trillion market valuation, mostly because of its weight loss drugs. Novo Nordisk's entire national economy in Denmark bends around the performance of a single injection pen. But now Eli Lilly’s scientists are looking for the next ceiling to break. And it seems like everything is pointing towards that pesky weight loss plateau.

segments.titre: Retatrutide LY3437943 and the Phase 2 question
segments.resume: Retatrutide, coded LY3437943, was engineered by Lilly to break the ceiling capping every drug in the category. When the New England Journal of Medicine published the Phase 2 data in June 2023, the question was whether the body would respond to the third signal.
segments.texte: The fruits of its labors, designated LY3437943 in Eli Lilly’s labs, was eventually named retatrutide. It is the product of a company that watched its rival win the first round of a trillion-dollar war, identified the exact biological ceiling that was capping every drug in the category, and spent years engineering a molecule specifically designed to break through it. Eli Lilly could explain the triple-receptor theory all day long, but pharmaceutical history is littered with elegant mechanisms that fell apart the moment they met real human bodies in a controlled trial. So in June 2023, when the New England Journal of Medicine published the Phase 2 data, the entire endocrinology world was really asking one question: does the city actually listen to all three orders, or does it find a way to ignore the third one the way it's ignored every other intervention before it?

segments.titre: Phase 2 results beat Wegovy and Mounjaro
segments.resume: At the highest dose retatrutide outperformed the best results ever recorded for Wegovy and Mounjaro, ranking first in a review of twelve GLP-1 class drugs across over 15,000 patients. Phase 2 is promising but only Phase 3 is bigger, longer and harder to game.
segments.texte: Then the data came back. And it wasn’t even close. At the highest dose tested, Retatrutide outpaced the best results ever recorded for both Wegovy and Mounjaro by a wide enough margin that a head-to-head review of twelve different GLP-1 class drugs, spanning over 15,000 patients, ranked it first by a clear distance. Phase 2 is promising, but it isn’t proof either. The real test is Phase 3, which is bigger, longer, and harder to game.

segments.titre: Phase 3 TRIUMPH-4 and TRIUMPH-1 results
segments.resume: TRIUMPH-4 in December 2025 reported 28.7% average weight loss at 68 weeks. TRIUMPH-1, the FDA-supporting trial of over 2,300 double-blind participants, showed 28.3% at 80 weeks and 30.3% at 104 weeks, about 85 pounds, reaching surgical-level weight loss.
segments.texte: In December 2025, the first Phase 3 readout was published under the fitting title, TRIUMPH-4. Eli Lilly reported 28.7% average weight loss at 68 weeks. Then, several months later came the trial that actually matters most: TRIUMPH-1. This was the crucial study Eli Lilly built specifically to support its FDA application. It had over 2,300 participants tested double-blind against a placebo. At 80 weeks, the highest dose averaged 28.3% weight loss. And for the people who stayed on it through 104 weeks, that number climbed to 30.3%, or an average of 85 pounds, gone, from a once-weekly shot. The majority, then, reached surgical-level weight loss. That’s proof that the drug is

segments.titre: Secondary benefits: liver fat, blood pressure and no plateau
segments.resume: A substudy in the New England Journal of Medicine found an 82.4% liver fat reduction by MRI at 12 mg in 24 weeks, the greatest ever recorded, and TRIUMPH-4 showed a 14-point systolic blood pressure drop. No plateau appeared in any trial, shifting the question to what happens after years with the body's defenses switched off.
segments.texte: operating on another level entirely, and the secondary findings keep compounding. A substudy published in the New England Journal of Medicine measuring liver fat directly by MRI found an 82.4% reduction at the 12 milligram dose in 24 weeks, the most potent liver fat reduction ever recorded for any drug, in a disease that affects roughly one in three adults worldwide. TRIUMPH-4 showed a 14-point drop in systolic blood pressure, the kind of number that would justify a dedicated blood pressure medication on its own. The shape of the curve should matter here. Every weight-loss intervention in history eventually plateaus. Across every Retatrutide trial published so far, researchers explicitly noted no plateau. The body never found its footing. That’s the difference between an impressive drug and a paradigm break. And it's also why, by the time TRIUMPH-1 dropped, the real question in the room had changed from whether it worked or not to what does a body look like after years with its defenses against fat loss switched off?

segments.titre: Cardiac risks: heart rate and the missing outcomes trial
segments.resume: Because glucagon is chronotropic, the highest dose in Phase 2 raised resting heart rate by 6.7 beats per minute, with irregular heartbeats in 2 to 11% versus about 2% on placebo. The cardiovascular outcomes trial is still running, so no five-year cardiac data exist, the biggest open question.
segments.texte: Every drug this powerful comes with a cost, and Retatrutide's costs split into two very different categories. One kind shows up in a clinical trial, gets measured, gets a percentage attached to it. The other kind only shows up after the trial ends, after the drug leaves the lab, and the real world starts doing whatever it wants with it. Let’s start with what the data actually shows. Glucagon is naturally what doctors call chronotropic, meaning that it is something that speeds up the heart. So if you're cranking the body's furnaces up to maximum, it makes sense that the whole thermal plant starts running hotter too. In Phase 2 trials, the highest dose raised participants' resting heart rate by an average of 6.7 beats per minute, and irregular heartbeats showed up in roughly 2 to 11% of people taking the drug, compared to about 2% on placebo. For most healthy adults, that's not something to lose sleep over. For someone who already has heart disease, it might be a real problem, and the dedicated cardiovascular outcomes trial that would actually answer that question is still running. Nobody has the five-year cardiac picture yet, and that missing piece is probably the single biggest question mark hanging over this entire drug.

segments.titre: Muscle loss: about 35% of weight lost is lean mass
segments.resume: Retatrutide's furnaces burn muscle as well as fat: in the highest-dose group about 35% of lost weight was lean muscle, more without resistance training. Protein intake and weight lifting determine what is lost, with weakness a particular danger for older adults.
segments.texte: Then there’s muscle. When you tell the body's furnaces to burn everything in storage, they don't politely sort fat from muscle on the way out. In the highest-dose group, roughly 35% of the total weight participants lost was actually lean muscle mass. If you skip resistance training entirely, that number can climb even higher. The drug handles the burning, clearly. What gets burned is largely up to the person taking it, depending on how much protein they eat, whether they're lifting weights, whether they're paying attention to anything besides the number on the scale. Ignore that part of the equation, and you can end up 60 pounds lighter and noticeably weaker at the same time. Never a good outcome, especially in older adults.

segments.titre: Dysesthesia: a new side effect unique to retatrutide
segments.resume: Phase 2 trials revealed dysesthesia, tingling, numbness or burning without a cause, in 8 to 10% of participants at the highest dose, found nowhere else in the GLP-1 class. It is mostly mild and likely linked to glucagon receptors on nerves, but needs years of follow-up.
segments.texte: And then there’s the side effects nobody saw coming. Phase 2 trials turned up something that doesn't exist anywhere else in this entire drug class, a sensation called dysesthesia. This is a tingling, numbness, or burning with no actual cause touching the skin, and it showed up in 8 to 10% of participants at the highest dose. Most cases are mild, and it rarely makes anyone quit the drug, but it's a genuinely new finding, likely connected to glucagon receptors sitting on nerves throughout the body. Exactly the kind of thing that takes years of follow-up data to fully understand.

segments.titre: FDA rules: retatrutide cannot be compounded and warning letters
segments.resume: Retatrutide cannot legally be compounded because the shortage-list loophole used for semaglutide and tirzepatide does not apply to an unapproved drug. The FDA sent over fifty warning letters in September 2025 and in April 2026 targeted retail sites like Gram Peptides and Prime Sciences, saying a 'research use only' label changes nothing.
segments.texte: What’s more, under current FDA rules, Retatrutide can’t legally be compounded at all, full stop. Semaglutide and tirzepatide had a legal loophole for years; when a brand-name drug sits on the FDA's official shortage list, compounding pharmacies are allowed to make their own versions of it. Retatrutide has never had an approved version to be in shortage from in the first place, so there's no exemption to claim. Selling it for human use is simply illegal, and the FDA has said exactly that, in writing, more than once. In September 2025, the agency sent over fifty warning letters to compounders and websites selling unapproved GLP-1 products, and several of those letters named retatrutide specifically. By April 2026, the FDA had moved past pharmacies entirely and started going after ordinary retail websites like Gram Peptides and Prime Sciences, both of which were caught selling retatrutide labeled "research use only." The agency made it clear that disclaimer doesn't mean anything the moment a product page starts describing appetite suppression and weight loss. In the FDA's own words, slapping "not for human consumption" on a label doesn't change what's actually in the vial, or what the seller is quietly implying you'll do with it.

segments.titre: Waves of FDA letters and adverse event reports
segments.resume: More FDA letters followed in March and June 2026, hitting manufacturers, compounders and direct-selling websites in turn. By May 2026 the FDA had logged over 1,700 adverse event reports tied to compounded GLP-1 products, a pattern common to unregulated peptides injected at home without oversight.
segments.texte: But the letters keep coming in waves. 30 more in March 2026, 25 more in June. Each wave hit a different layer of the supply chain. First the manufacturers, then the compounding pharmacies, then the websites selling directly to whoever's willing to pay. By May 2026, the FDA had logged more than 1,700 adverse event reports tied to compounded GLP-1 products. Naturally, that’s the broader category of unregulated peptides, but the pattern repeats itself every time products get made outside any verified manufacturing process and then get sold to people injecting themselves at home with absolutely zero clinical oversight if something goes wrong.

segments.titre: The gray market: biohackers, gym users and looksmaxxers
